title: Intussusception
subject: Surgery
summary: Intussusception is telescoping of one bowel segment into another, causing obstruction. In children it is often idiopathic; in adults a lead point is common. Prompt diagnosis and reduction are essential to prevent ischemia.

sections.p: A segment of intestine (intussusceptum) slides into the adjacent distal segment (intussuscipiens), creating a bowel obstruction that can compromise blood flow.
b: Classic triad: intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, red‑currant jelly stool (rare).
Palpable sausage‑shaped mass in the right upper quadrant or periumbilical area.

t.b: Confirms intussusception and shows location; if positive, proceed to reduction.
Both diagnostic and therapeutic; demonstrates filling defect and may reduce the intussusception.
Looks for gasless abdomen or fluid‑filled loops; useful when ultrasound unavailable.

sections.p: Severity is judged by duration of symptoms, presence of peritonitis, and signs of bowel ischemia.
b: Stage I: transient, no perforation, viable bowel.
Stage II: persistent obstruction, bowel still viable.
Stage III: bowel necrosis or perforation – surgical emergency.

sections.p: Causes differ by age and setting.
b: Children (0‑2 y): idiopathic (hypertrophied Peyer’s patches after viral infection, especially adenovirus).
Children in low‑resource settings: Meckel’s diverticulum, intestinal lymphoid hyperplasia from malaria or HIV.
Adults: tumour (benign or malignant), postoperative adhesions, Crohn’s disease, intestinal polyps, tuberculosis stricture.

sections.p: Presentation evolves from intermittent colicky pain to constant pain with vomiting and possible bloody stool.
b: Sudden, severe abdominal pain with drawing up of legs.
Non‑bilious vomiting early, becoming bilious as obstruction progresses.
Stool that may be dark, tarry, or described as red‑currant jelly.

sections.p: Use bedside tools first; imaging follows based on availability.

t.b: Distinguishes intussusception from gastroenteritis or colic; look for pain pattern, vomiting, stool colour.
Shows target sign; if not available, proceed to plain X‑ray.
Provides both diagnosis and reduction; watch for perforation risk.
Detect dehydration, anemia from bleeding; guide fluid resuscitation.

sections.p: Identify early to avoid bowel necrosis.
b: Persistent abdominal tenderness with guarding or rebound.
Signs of peritonitis: fever, tachycardia, hypotension.
Bloody stool with hemodynamic instability.

sections.p: Stabilise, then attempt non‑operative reduction; surgery if that fails or complications arise.
b: IV fluids and electrolyte correction before any procedure.
Pneumatic or hydrostatic (saline) enema under fluoroscopy or ultrasound guidance – first‑line in children without perforation.
Surgical reduction (laparotomy or laparoscopy) if enema fails, perforation suspected, or adult with lead point.
Resect non‑viable bowel and send pathology if tumour suspected.

sections.p: Monitor for recurrence and address underlying cause.
b: Observe for 24 h after successful reduction; repeat ultrasound if pain recurs.
In children with Meckel’s diverticulum or pathological lead point, plan elective surgery.
Educate caregivers on early signs of obstruction.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic colicky pain and vomiting.
b: Acute gastroenteritis – usually watery stool, no palpable mass.
Volvulus – may have similar obstruction but lacks target sign on ultrasound.
Hernia incarceration – external bulge, often reducible.
Early intussusception may not show classic target sign on ultrasound; repeat if suspicion high.
Contrast enema can be normal if reduction already occurred spontaneously.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe, unrelenting abdominal pain with guarding
Vomiting that becomes bilious or profuse
Bloody stool with signs of shock

faq.q: Why is intussusception more common in infants than adults?
faq.a: Infants have abundant lymphoid tissue that can swell after viral infections, creating a lead point; adults usually need a structural lesion.

faq.q: Can a plain X‑ray diagnose intussusception?
faq.a: It may show a gasless abdomen or fluid‑filled loops but cannot confirm intussusception; ultrasound is preferred.

faq.q: What is the role of surgery in children?
faq.a: Surgery is reserved for failed non‑operative reduction, perforation, or when a pathological lead point is identified.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect intussusception over gastroenteritis? — Intermittent colicky pain, palpable sausage‑shaped mass, and possible red‑currant jelly stool.
How does ultrasound differentiate intussusception from simple bowel loops? — Shows concentric rings (target sign) indicating telescoped bowel.
A child presents with vomiting and a palpable mass; ultrasound is unavailable. What is your next step? — Obtain a contrast enema, which can both diagnose and reduce the intussusception.
Why is pneumatic reduction preferred to hydrostatic in many centres? — Air is radiolucent, allowing clear fluoroscopic visualization and lower risk of electrolyte disturbance.
An adult with intussusception is found to have a tumour on imaging. What is the definitive management? — Surgical resection of the involved segment with oncologic margins.
What signs indicate progression to bowel necrosis requiring emergency surgery? — Persistent tenderness, guarding, fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and peritoneal signs.
How would HIV infection increase the risk of intussusception in children? — HIV‑related lymphoid hyperplasia creates a lead point in the ileum.
After successful enema reduction, what follow‑up is essential? — Observe for at least 24 h, repeat ultrasound if pain recurs, and assess for underlying lead point.
